items.context: Slack, asking a teammate for a hand at the end of the day.

explain_es.analogy: Un favor es una tarea que hacés por otro, no algo que creás de la nada.
explain_es.rule: "Do someone a favour" es fijo: el favor se hace con do.
explain_es.why: En castellano decís "hacerme un favor" y el "hacer" no te dice cuál elegir. En inglés es do, siempre, y la persona va en el medio: do me a favour.

options: make
do
take
items.rule: Do someone a favour. Fixed phrase.
items.text: Could you ___ me a favour and review this before you log off?

items.context: Slack, telling your lead the sprint is on track.

explain_es.analogy: El progreso aparece donde antes no había nada. Lo que aparece se produce, y producir es make.
explain_es.rule: "Make progress" es fijo, como make a decision o make a change.
explain_es.why: "Hacer progreso" tira para do porque suena a tarea, pero el par correcto es "make progress". Aparece en toda daily y en todo mail de estado, así que conviene tenerlo automatizado.

items.rule: Make progress, never do progress.
items.text: We did good progress on the importer this week, it's almost done.

items.context: Slack, asking a teammate.

explain_es.analogy: Do es para "ejecutar" una tarea del backlog; make es para "producir" algo que antes no existía.
explain_es.rule: Do va con tareas y actividades: do a review, do some research, do the testing.
explain_es.why: Un code review es una tarea que ejecutás, así que es do. "Make a code review" es un calco de "hacer" y suena raro.

items.rule: Do is for tasks, jobs and work: do a review, do the dishes, do some testing.
items.text: Can you ___ a quick code review before lunch?

items.context: Planning meeting, before committing to a date.

explain_es.analogy: Es el ticket del backlog que alguien va a agarrar. Ejecutar un ticket es do; inventar algo nuevo es make.
explain_es.rule: Do va con el trabajo que ejecutás: do research, do testing, do a review.
explain_es.why: "Make research" es el calco de "hacer una investigación" y suena mal en inglés. La investigación es una tarea, y las tareas van con do.

items.rule: Do research, do testing, do a review: work you carry out goes with do.
items.text: Before we commit to a date, someone has to ___ some research on their API.

items.context: Negotiating a late change with a client.

explain_es.analogy: La excepción no estaba en el contrato hasta que la decís. La estás produciendo en ese momento.
explain_es.rule: Make an exception, make an offer, make a suggestion: todo lo que creás de la nada va con make.
explain_es.why: No es una tarea del backlog, es algo nuevo que aparece porque vos lo ofreciste. Por eso va make y no do.

options: take
make
do
items.rule: Make an exception, make an offer, make a suggestion: you create something that did not exist.
items.text: We can ___ an exception this time, but the next change goes into phase two.

items.context: A junior asks you how to raise a doubt during the daily.

explain_es.analogy: Hay una salida más que el castellano te esconde. "Hacer" cubre tanto que a veces la respuesta no es ni make ni do.
explain_es.rule: Una pregunta no se hace con make ni con do. Se pregunta, y el verbo es ask.
explain_es.why: "Hacer una pregunta" es "ask a question". Este error se nota mucho porque en una daily preguntás todos los días, así que lo repetís todas las mañanas.

options: Can I do a question about the deploy?
Can I ask a question about the deploy?
Can I make a question about the deploy?
items.rule: A question is asked, not made and not done. Ask a question, ask for something.
items.text: Which one is right when you want to ask something in the daily?

items.context: Sprint review with a client.

explain_es.analogy: Make escribe una migración nueva; do la corre. Una crea el archivo, la otra ejecuta el comando.
explain_es.rule: Make es traer algo a la existencia; do es ejecutar trabajo que ya estaba definido.
explain_es.why: El cambio de esquema no existía hasta que lo hiciste: make. La corrida de regresión ya estaba en el checklist y sólo la ejecutaste: do. No tiene que ver con que una cosa dure más, ni con el singular y el plural.

options: A change is something you produce; a run is a task you carry out.
The schema is a thing, so it takes "make" wherever it appears.
"Make" goes with singular nouns and "do" with plural ones.
A change is permanent and a run is temporary, so they differ.
items.question: Why "made a change" but "did a regression run"?
items.rule: Make = bring something into existence. Do = perform work that was already defined.
items.text: We made a change to the schema and then did a full regression run.

items.context: Proposal for a client, describing your release process.

explain_es.analogy: Es una tarea del checklist de release, no algo que inventás. Los pasos del checklist se ejecutan.
explain_es.rule: "Do a round of testing" o "run a round of testing". El testing es trabajo que ejecutás.
explain_es.why: "Make a round of testing" es el calco de "hacer una ronda de testing". Va do, o run si querés sonar más técnico. Fijate el contraste con "make a change", donde sí creás algo nuevo.

items.rule: Do a round of testing. Testing is work you perform, so it takes do (or run).
items.text: Before every release we make a round of manual testing on staging.

items.context: Sprint review with a client.

explain_es.analogy: Es como una convención de nombres en un framework: tiene una lógica general, pero hay casos históricos que simplemente se memorizan.
explain_es.rule: La idea general: make es producir o crear, do es ejecutar una tarea. Pero muchos pares son fijos y se aprenden como bloque.
explain_es.why: La documentación es una tarea (do). "Make progress" es un par fijo. No tiene que ver con el tiempo verbal ni con el tamaño de la cosa, y no son intercambiables: "do progress" está mal.

options: Make goes with finished results and do with tasks that are still in progress.
Make is for big achievements and do for the small routine tasks nobody notices.
Make is for producing a result and do for tasks, but many pairs are fixed chunks.
They are interchangeable; the sentence alternates them only to avoid repetition.
items.question: Why "made progress" but "do the documentation"?
items.rule: General idea: make = create or produce; do = perform a task. Fixed pairs (make progress, do business) are learned as chunks.
items.text: We made a lot of progress, but we still have to do the documentation.

items.context: Retro, talking about how the incident was handled.

explain_es.analogy: Es el árbitro que cobra el penal: alguien tiene que señalar, y después se come el quilombo. Por eso "the call" y no "a call".
explain_es.rule: "Make the call" es tomar la decisión y bancársela. "Make a call" con "a" es llamar por teléfono.
explain_es.why: El artículo cambia todo el significado. Acá el problema del postmortem no fue que nadie llamara a nadie ni que faltara gente en la llamada: fue que nadie se hizo cargo de decidir el rollback.

options: Decide, and own the decision nobody else wanted.
Do the work of rolling the release back by hand.
Phone the client to warn them about the outage.
Raise the alarm so the whole team joins the call.
items.question: What does "make the call" mean here?
items.rule: Make the call = take the decision, and be the one responsible for it. Make a call = phone someone.
items.text: Nobody wanted to make the call to roll back, so we lost twenty minutes.

items.context: Slack, waiting for a build.

explain_es.analogy: Tell tiene un destinatario obligatorio, como un email que necesita "to:". Say es publicar algo sin destinatario explícito.
explain_es.rule: Tell va seguido de la persona que escucha: tell me. Say va con lo que se dice.
explain_es.why: Después viene "me", la persona, así que va tell. "Say me" es el error típico por "decime". Las dos formas con preposición fallan cada una por su lado: tell ya lleva la persona pegada y nunca admite to delante de ella ("tell to me" no existe en ningún contexto); y "say to me", que sí existe cuando repetís palabras ("he said to me that…"), acá no entra, porque no estás pidiendo que te repitan algo dicho, estás pidiendo un aviso, y avisar es territorio de tell.

options: tell to
say
tell
say to
items.rule: Tell + person: tell me, tell the client. Say + words: say something, say that…
items.text: Can you ___ me when the build is green?

items.context: End of standup.

explain_es.analogy: Lo que decís es literalmente "thank you": son las palabras, no el destinatario. Por eso es say.
explain_es.rule: Say va con expresiones como say thank you, say hello o say sorry.
explain_es.why: "Tell thank you" está mal porque tell necesita una persona pegada, y acá lo que viene es lo que decís, no a quién. Y "tell you thanks" no es una versión más pobre de lo mismo: no se dice, no la vas a escuchar nunca. Si querés nombrar a quién le agradecés, el inglés te lo pide con preposición: "say thank you to someone", o "thank someone" directamente.

items.rule: Fixed phrases with say: say thank you, say hello, say sorry.
items.text: I just wanted to ___ thank you for covering my on-call shift.

items.context: Standup, reporting what the client answered yesterday.

explain_es.analogy: Tell es un mensaje directo, con destinatario en el "para". Say es un log sin destinatario.
explain_es.rule: Si la persona que escucha va pegada al verbo, es tell.
explain_es.why: "Us" es la persona y está pegada al verbo, así que va "told us". "Said us" no existe; lo más parecido sería "said to us", con el to en el medio.

items.rule: The listener comes right after the verb, so it has to be tell: told us.
items.text: She ___ us that the credentials will be ready on Thursday.

items.context: Incident channel, checking who has been informed.

explain_es.analogy: Tell es "enviar a"; say es "publicar". Si hay un destinatario nombrado, casi siempre es tell.
explain_es.rule: Tell lleva la persona pegada y después el mensaje. Say necesita un "to" antes de la persona.
explain_es.why: "The client" es la persona que escucha y va justo después del verbo, así que va tell. "Say the client" no existe, y "say to the client that…" es correcto pero suena forzado acá.

options: tell
say
say to
items.rule: Tell + person + that. Say needs "to" before the person: say to the client.
items.text: Did anyone ___ the client that the export is down?

items.context: Update to your team after a client call.

explain_es.analogy: Say sin destinatario es como un log; tell es un mensaje directo. Si hay un "us" pegado, es un DM: told.
explain_es.rule: Si la persona que escucha va pegada al verbo, es tell: told us.
explain_es.why: Lo correcto es "told us". También valdría "said to us" o "said that", pero con "said us" no existe.

items.rule: If the listener comes right after the verb, use tell: told us. Say needs "to": said to us.
items.text: The client said us that the deadline can't move.

items.context: Retro, being honest about how the estimate went.

explain_es.analogy: Son excepciones grabadas a fuego, como los verbos irregulares. No se deducen de la regla, se memorizan.
explain_es.rule: Hay frases congeladas que son de tell aunque no haya persona: tell the truth, tell a lie, tell the difference.
explain_es.why: "Say the truth" es calco de "decir la verdad" y no se usa. La regla general pediría say porque no hay persona, pero estas frases van con tell igual.

items.rule: Fixed phrases with tell and no listener: tell the truth, tell a lie, tell the difference.
items.text: Let's ___ the truth, the estimate was optimistic from day one.

items.context: Reporting to your team what your lead decided.

explain_es.analogy: Pensá en dos funciones con firmas distintas: say(message) y tell(person, message). Si no pasás la persona, tell no compila.
explain_es.rule: Say va con el mensaje y sin persona. Tell siempre necesita una persona en el medio.
explain_es.why: Sin persona nombrada, el verbo es say. "Said me" es el calco de "me dijo" y es el error más frecuente de todos. "Told that" falla al revés: tell quedó sin su persona.

options: He said me that the release can wait until Monday.
He said that the release can wait until Monday.
He told that the release can wait until Monday.
items.rule: Say + that (no listener). Tell always needs a listener: told me that…
items.text: Which one is right?

items.context: A client wants the commitment in writing.

explain_es.analogy: Acá el objeto es el contenido ("that"), no una persona. El contenido es territorio de say.
explain_es.rule: Say va con las palabras que se dicen. Sin una persona pegada al verbo, tell no entra.
explain_es.why: "Tell that in an email" no funciona porque falta la persona. Si la nombraras, sí sería tell: "tell them that in an email". Y "talk" no lleva objeto directo nunca.

options: tell
talk
say
items.rule: Say + the words. Without a listener right after the verb, tell is impossible.
items.text: Could you ___ that in an email so I can forward it to my boss?

items.context: Reporting a client meeting to your team.

explain_es.analogy: Tell tiene el destinatario en la firma; say lo acepta sólo si lo envolvés en un "to". Es un parámetro con nombre.
explain_es.rule: Tell alguien algo. Say algo a alguien, con to. La diferencia es esa preposición.
explain_es.why: "Us" está pegado al verbo, y ahí sólo entra tell. Say sí puede llevar persona, pero con to ("said to us"), así que la opción del "nunca" es falsa. Tampoco depende de si la noticia es mala ni de que aparezca "that".

options: There is no "that" in the sentence, so you must use "tell".
"Said" can never be followed by a person in any sentence.
"Told" is used for bad news and "said" for neutral information.
The listener comes right after the verb, and only "tell" allows it.
items.question: Why "told us" and not "said us"?
items.rule: Tell someone something. Say something to someone. The difference is the "to".
items.text: They told us the budget is frozen until the new quarter starts.

items.context: Passing on an instruction your lead gave you.

explain_es.analogy: Una orden necesita a quién va dirigida, como un ticket necesita assignee. Tell trae ese campo; say no.
explain_es.rule: Para pasar una instrucción es "tell someone to do something". Say no admite ni la persona pegada ni ese infinitivo.
explain_es.why: "Said me" es el calco directo de "me dijo" y es el error que más se escucha. Acá además hay un infinitivo ("to freeze"), y esa construcción es exclusiva de tell.

items.rule: Tell someone to do something. Say cannot take a person or an infinitive like this.
items.text: Marina said me to freeze the branch until the audit is over.

items.context: Incident update in a meeting.

explain_es.analogy: Tell es el mensaje con destinatario; say es el contenido. Si nombrás a quién, casi siempre es tell.
explain_es.rule: Tell lleva la persona pegada (tell someone); say va directo a lo dicho (say that...).
explain_es.why: En "told the client" aparece la persona, así que es tell; en "said that" no hay persona, así que es say. No es por órdenes vs. información, formalidad ni tiempo verbal.

options: Tell needs the listener right after it (tell someone); say doesn't (say something).
Said reports a general statement and told is the one used for future promises.
Tell is for giving orders and say is for passing neutral information to someone.
Told sounds more formal, so it is the one that fits when you talk to a client.
items.question: Why "told the client" but "said that"?
items.rule: Tell someone something. Say something (to someone).
items.text: She said that the API was down, and she told the client it would be fixed soon.

items.context: Writing up a postmortem.

explain_es.analogy: Un cartel, un mail y un log también "say" cosas. Lo que no pueden hacer es "tell" al aire, sin nadie del otro lado.
explain_es.rule: Lo que decide el verbo es si hay una persona que escucha justo después, no quién habla.
explain_es.why: La alerta no le habla a nadie en particular, así que va said. Un objeto sí puede ser sujeto de tell si nombrás al que escucha: "the docs tell you how to configure it". Y no tiene nada que ver con el tiempo verbal ni con que sea escrito u oral.

options: An alert is not a person, so it cannot be the subject of "tell".
"Say" only needs the words; "tell" needs a person to receive them.
Written sources take "say" and spoken ones take "tell" instead.
"Said" is the past of "say" and this sentence is in the past.
items.question: Why can an alert "say" something but not "tell" it here?
items.rule: What decides the verb is whether a listener follows it, not who is speaking.
items.text: The alert said the queue was empty, but nobody told the on-call engineer.

items.context: Slack, quoting what the client answered about the invoice.

explain_es.analogy: Es tell con un parámetro faltante: o le agregás la persona, o cambiás de función.
explain_es.rule: Tell necesita una persona entre el verbo y el mensaje. Si no la nombrás, va say.
explain_es.why: Acá no hay nadie que escuche nombrado, así que el arreglo de una palabra es "said that". La otra salida sería agregar la persona y decir "told us that", pero eso ya cambia dos cosas.

items.rule: Tell needs a listener between the verb and the message. With no listener, use say.
items.text: The client told that the invoice is already approved on their side.

blocks.body_en: In English, "the" points at something both of us already have in mind. If you are not pointing at anything in particular, you use nothing at all. That is the whole rule, and it is why "users don't read error messages" and "the users don't read the error messages" are two different sentences: the second one is about a specific group, probably the ones in this project.
blocks.body_es: En inglés "the" es un dedo que señala algo que los dos ya tenemos en la cabeza. Si no estás señalando nada en particular, no va nada. En castellano decís "los usuarios" hasta para hablar de todos los usuarios del mundo, y ese "los" no se traduce. Ahí nace el calco: metés un "the" que en inglés cambia de qué estás hablando.
examples: Users don't read error messages.
Security is not a nice-to-have for a fintech client.
I've been writing software since 2013.

blocks.body_en: No article with plural nouns used in general (clients, deadlines, tests), with uncountable and abstract nouns used in general (security, feedback, documentation, software, performance), and inside a short list of fixed expressions about everyday places and channels. One warning: a singular countable noun can never stand alone. It is "a client" or "the client" or "clients", never just "client".
blocks.body_es: Sin artículo en tres casos. Uno, plurales en general (clients, deadlines, tests). Dos, incontables y abstractos en general (security, feedback, documentation, software, performance). Tres, un puñado de expresiones fijas de lugares y canales, que se aprenden de memoria. Y un aviso: un sustantivo contable en singular nunca va solo. Es "a client", "the client" o "clients", pero nunca "client" pelado.
examples: Most clients care more about dates than about the stack.
Documentation is part of the definition of done.
I work from home on Fridays and go to the office on Tuesdays.
It only fails in production, never on my machine.
I'll send you the numbers by email before six.
We page the on-call engineer at night.
blocks.title_en: The three places where nothing goes

blocks.body_en: Each pair is the same sentence with and without "the". Both are correct English; they are about different things, and in a client call that difference is the whole message.
blocks.body_es: Cada par es la misma oración con y sin "the". Las dos están bien escritas: hablan de cosas distintas. En una reunión con un cliente, esa diferencia es todo el mensaje.

pairs.a: Users don't read error messages.
pairs.b: The users don't read the error messages.
pairs.difference_es: La primera habla de los usuarios en general, de cualquier producto. La segunda habla de unos usuarios concretos y de unos mensajes concretos, los de esta app. Si querías decir la primera y dijiste la segunda, el cliente entiende que estás hablando de los suyos.

pairs.a: Security is the priority this quarter.
pairs.b: The security of the payments API is the priority this quarter.
pairs.difference_es: Sin artículo, "security" es el tema, el área de trabajo. Con "the" pedís que digas de qué, y por eso la segunda termina en "of the payments API". Un "the security" suelto deja al que escucha esperando un complemento que nunca llega.

pairs.a: We deployed to production last night.
pairs.b: We deployed to the production cluster last night.
pairs.difference_es: "Production" como ambiente va pelado, igual que "staging". Con "the" ya no es el ambiente sino una cosa concreta, el cluster, y por eso aparece el sustantivo al lado.

pairs.a: She's at work until six.
pairs.b: She's at the office until six.
pairs.difference_es: "At work" es una expresión fija que significa "trabajando", y no lleva artículo nunca. "At the office" es un lugar físico y sí lo lleva. Son dos frases distintas, y "at the work" no existe en ninguna de las dos.

blocks.title_en: One word in, one word out

blocks.body_en: Every one of these is the Spanish article coming along for the ride. Read them out loud once with the extra word and once without; the version without is the one that sounds like a native.
blocks.body_es: Todos estos son el artículo del castellano que se vino de colado. Leelos en voz alta con la palabra de más y sin ella. La versión sin artículo es la que suena nativa.
examples: The life is hard when you're on call. ✗ → Life is hard when you're on call.
I have a good relationship with the clients. ✗ → I have a good relationship with clients.
The security is important for us. ✗ → Security is important for us.
I'm going to the work now. ✗ → I'm going to work now.
Send it to me by the email. ✗ → Send it to me by email.
In the general, users hate popups. ✗ → In general, users hate popups.
Client cares more about dates. ✗ → Clients care more about dates.

blocks.body_en: Learn these whole. Every one of them is a place where a Spanish speaker adds a "the" and an English speaker doesn't.
blocks.body_es: Aprendelas enteras. En todas, un hispanohablante mete un "the" y un angloparlante no.
examples: In general, clients care about dates more than about the stack.
Security is part of the definition of done.
Documentation is part of the ticket, not a separate one.
It only happens in production.
I'm on call this week.
I work from home on Fridays.
I'll confirm by email before the end of the day.
We don't do estimates in hours for projects this size.
Life as a team lead is mostly meetings and unblocking people.
Good software takes longer than anyone wants to hear.

lessons.goal_en: Talk about users, security and software in general without putting "the" in front of them.
lessons.title_en: When English uses no article at all

blocks.body_en: When something breaks, everyone wants the same three answers, in the same order: what is happening, what you already did, and what happens next. English has a fixed set of phrases for each one. Learn the phrases and the hard part stops being the language and goes back to being the bug.
blocks.body_es: Ante un incidente, todos quieren las mismas tres respuestas y en el mismo orden: qué está pasando, qué hiciste ya y qué sigue. El inglés tiene frases fijas para cada una. Si las tenés listas, lo difícil vuelve a ser el bug y no el idioma.
examples: We're seeing elevated error rates on checkout.
We've rolled back the release and the errors are gone.
We're monitoring and we'll send another update in 30 minutes.

blocks.body_en: Present continuous for what is happening now, present perfect for what you already did and whose result matters, past simple for the story once it's over, and will or going to for the next step. Each tense answers one of the three questions.
blocks.body_es: Presente continuo para lo que está pasando ahora, present perfect para lo que ya hiciste y cuyo resultado importa, pasado simple para contar la historia una vez cerrada, y will o going to para el próximo paso. Cada tiempo contesta una de las tres preguntas.
examples: We're investigating a spike in 500s on the payments API.
We've identified the cause and deployed a fix.
The root cause was an expired certificate on the load balancer.
We'll publish a full postmortem tomorrow.
blocks.title_en: The tense does half the work

blocks.body_en: English incident reports describe systems, not people. Read each pair: the facts are identical, but only one version can be pasted into a client channel.
blocks.body_es: Un reporte de incidente en inglés habla de sistemas, no de personas. En cada par los hechos son los mismos, pero sólo una versión se puede pegar en el canal del cliente.

pairs.a: Mateo pushed a bad config and took the site down.
pairs.b: A config change brought the site down.
pairs.difference_es: La primera señala a una persona y te deja discutiendo culpas. La segunda cuenta lo mismo poniendo el foco en el cambio, que es lo que se arregla.

pairs.a: The database failed and we don't know why.
pairs.b: We've narrowed it down to the database and we're still investigating.
pairs.difference_es: Las dos admiten que no sabés la causa. La segunda además muestra avance, y eso es lo que hace que el cliente te siga esperando.

pairs.a: It's fixed.
pairs.b: We've deployed a fix and the error rate is back to normal.
pairs.difference_es: "It's fixed" obliga al otro a preguntar cómo sabés que está arreglado. La segunda trae el arreglo y la evidencia en la misma frase.

pairs.a: We had an incident yesterday and we're investigating it.
pairs.b: We had an incident yesterday and we've closed it out.
pairs.difference_es: El pasado simple cierra la historia, así que mezclarlo con "we're investigating" suena raro: si ya terminó, contá el cierre.

blocks.title_en: The same fact, with and without blame

blocks.body_en: Four of these come from translating the Spanish word straight across, and each one lands in a client channel sooner or later.
blocks.body_es: Cuatro salen de traducir la palabra del castellano tal cual, y todas terminan tarde o temprano en un canal con el cliente.
examples: We'll send an actualization. ✗ → We'll send an update.
The service is down since 10:00. ✗ → The service has been down since 10:00.
We are going to revert the deploy. ✓ but shorter: We're rolling it back.
Sorry for the inconveniences. ✗ → Sorry for the inconvenience. (uncountable)
It resulted that the cache was stale. ✗ → It turned out the cache was stale.

blocks.body_en: Copy these into your incident template. They cover the whole arc, from the first alert to the postmortem.
blocks.body_es: Pegalas en tu plantilla de incidentes. Cubren todo el arco, desde la primera alerta hasta el postmortem.
examples: We're aware of the issue and we're looking into it.
We've identified the root cause and we're working on a fix.
As a workaround, you can use the old export screen.
The impact was limited to users on the EU region.
We're monitoring closely and I'll update you in an hour.
Here's what we're doing to make sure it doesn't happen again.

lessons.goal_en: Report an outage so the client stays calm and nobody sounds blamed.

blocks.body_en: Every time you scope work with a client you're choosing between two "ifs". One says "this can really happen, and here's what I'll do". The other says "imagine this, but we both know it isn't on the table". Same word, two very different promises.
blocks.body_es: El primer condicional es un compromiso real: si pasa A, hago B. El segundo es hipotético: pinta un escenario que hoy no está sobre la mesa. En castellano los separás por el modo verbal sin pensarlo ("si aprobás" vs "si aprobaras"); en inglés el cambio está en el tiempo del verbo.
examples: If you approve the design today, we'll ship on Friday.
If we had another developer, we could ship on Friday.

blocks.body_en: First conditional: if + present, then will / can / may + verb. Second conditional: if + past, then would / could + verb. The past in a second conditional is not about the past: it marks distance from reality.
blocks.body_es: Primer condicional: if + presente, y en la otra mitad will, can o may. Segundo condicional: if + pasado, y en la otra mitad would o could. Ese pasado no habla del pasado: marca que es imaginario. "If I had time" es "si tuviera tiempo", hoy.
examples: If the client sends the credentials, we can start on Monday.
If the tests pass, I'll merge it before standup.
If I had more context, I would estimate it differently.
If they doubled the budget, we could hire a designer.

blocks.body_en: Read each pair out loud. The words barely change; what you're committing to changes completely.
blocks.body_es: Leé cada par en voz alta. Cambian dos palabras, pero lo que estás prometiendo cambia por completo. Ese es el ejercicio: notar la diferencia antes de elegir.

pairs.a: If you approve it today, we'll ship on Friday.
pairs.b: If you approved it today, we'd ship on Friday.
pairs.difference_es: La primera es un trato: lo aprobás y el viernes está. La segunda suena a que sabés que hoy no lo va a aprobar, y estás mostrando lo que se pierde.

pairs.a: If the migration fails, we roll back.
pairs.b: If the migration failed, we would roll back.
pairs.difference_es: La primera trata la falla como algo posible y ya tenés el plan. La segunda la trata como poco probable: es la respuesta tranquilizadora en una reunión.

pairs.a: If we hire someone, we can take the second project.
pairs.b: If we hired someone, we could take the second project.
pairs.difference_es: La primera implica que contratar está en los planes. La segunda lo pone como escenario: sirve para negociar sin comprometerte a contratar.

pairs.a: If it breaks in production, I'll fix it tonight.
pairs.b: If it broke in production, I'd fix it tonight.
pairs.difference_es: La primera es una promesa concreta que el cliente puede sostener. La segunda es una hipótesis, y un cliente puede escucharla como que no te estás comprometiendo.

blocks.body_en: Four mistakes show up again and again, and all four come from translating the Spanish sentence word by word.
blocks.body_es: Cuatro errores que salen de traducir literal del castellano. Los cuatro se escuchan enseguida y son fáciles de sacar.
examples: If you will approve it, we'll ship. ✗ → If you approve it, we'll ship.
If I would have time, I'd help. ✗ → If I had time, I'd help.
If the client would ask, tell them Friday. ✗ → If the client asks, tell them Friday.
We'll ship on Friday, if you approve it today. ✗ (no comma) → We'll ship on Friday if you approve it today.

blocks.body_en: These are ready to use in a call. Learn them whole: the grammar comes along for free.
blocks.body_es: Frases enteras para una reunión. Aprendelas como bloque: la gramática viene adentro y no la tenés que armar.
examples: If you can get us the credentials this week, we'll have it live by the 30th.
If anything blocks us, I'll flag it in the daily.
If we went that way, we'd need two more weeks.
I'd rather not commit to that unless the scope is frozen.
If it were up to me, I'd cut the reporting screen from this phase.

lessons.goal_en: Commit to a real deadline, and float an idea you're not committing to yet.

blocks.body_en: Two moments need this one: the postmortem, where you explain what would have prevented the outage, and the interview question "what would you do differently?". Both are about a past you can't change, so English marks it with a tense you never use for real events.
blocks.body_es: Hay dos momentos donde esto aparece sí o sí: el postmortem, cuando explicás qué habría evitado el incidente, y la pregunta de entrevista "¿qué harías distinto?". Los dos hablan de un pasado que ya no se puede cambiar, y el inglés lo marca con una forma que nunca usás para hechos reales.
examples: If we had tested on Safari, we would have caught it before the release.
If I had asked for more context, I would have estimated it differently.

blocks.body_en: If + had + past participle, then would have + past participle. Each half has its own piece and they never swap. You can start with either half; when the if-part comes second, the comma disappears.
blocks.body_es: If + had + participio de un lado, y would have + participio del otro. Cada mitad tiene su pieza y no se intercambian. Podés arrancar por cualquiera de las dos; si el if va al final, la coma desaparece.
examples: If the runbook had been up to date, we would have recovered in minutes.
We would have shipped on time if the scope had been frozen.
If I had known about the audit, I wouldn't have taken that shortcut.
Could have and might have work too: we might have caught it in review.
blocks.title_en: Had on one side, would have on the other

blocks.body_en: The difference is one word, and it changes whether you're talking about your situation today or about something that already went wrong.
blocks.body_es: La diferencia es una palabra, y cambia si estás hablando de cómo son las cosas hoy o de algo que ya salió mal. En una reunión con un cliente, esa palabra decide si estás describiendo un riesgo o admitiendo un error.

pairs.a: If we had a staging environment, we would test the migration there.
pairs.b: If we had had a staging environment, we would have tested it there.
pairs.difference_es: La primera dice que hoy no tenés staging. La segunda dice que en ese momento no lo tenías, y por eso la migración se probó en producción.

pairs.a: If the client signed off today, we would start tomorrow.
pairs.b: If the client had signed off on Friday, we would have started Monday.
pairs.difference_es: La primera es un escenario que todavía puede pasar. La segunda cuenta una oportunidad que ya se perdió: el viernes no firmó.

pairs.a: If I were the lead, I would change how we estimate.
pairs.b: If I had been the lead, I would have changed how we estimated.
pairs.difference_es: La primera es una opinión sobre hoy. La segunda habla de un proyecto que ya terminó, y es la forma que se usa en una entrevista para contar qué harías distinto.

pairs.a: We wouldn't be fixing this today if we had written tests back then.
pairs.b: We wouldn't have fixed this last week if you hadn't written tests.
pairs.difference_es: La primera es mixta: causa en el pasado, consecuencia hoy. Es la deuda técnica hablando. La segunda se queda entera en el pasado.

blocks.title_en: Second or third, and what each one admits

blocks.body_en: All four come from translating the Spanish sentence word by word, and the first one is by far the most common.
blocks.body_es: Los cuatro salen de traducir literal del castellano. El primero es, de lejos, el más frecuente, y es el que más se nota en un postmortem escrito.
examples: If we would have tested it, we'd have caught it. ✗ → If we had tested it, we'd have caught it.
We would of shipped on time. ✗ → We would have shipped on time.
If I had knew about the freeze… ✗ → If I had known about the freeze…
If the rollback had ran automatically… ✗ → If the rollback had run automatically…

blocks.body_en: Owning a mistake in English is mostly these five phrases. Learn them whole and you sound accountable instead of defensive.
blocks.body_es: Hacerse cargo de un error en inglés es, en la práctica, estas cinco frases. Aprendelas enteras: suenan a responsabilidad y no a excusa.
examples: Looking back, if we had caught it in review, the outage wouldn't have happened.
In hindsight, I would have escalated it sooner.
If I had known that earlier, I would have flagged it in the daily.
We should have tested that path before the release.
What would have helped is a smoke test on checkout.

lessons.goal_en: Explain what went wrong without making excuses, in a postmortem or an interview.

blocks.body_en: A grammar mistake makes you sound foreign. A false friend makes you say something you did not mean, and nobody stops you, because the sentence is perfectly good English. The client writes it down, agrees with it and acts on it. That is why these cost more than anything else on this list.
blocks.body_es: Un error de gramática te hace sonar extranjero. Un falso amigo te hace decir otra cosa, y nadie te frena, porque la oración es inglés impecable. El cliente lo anota, lo acepta y actúa en consecuencia. Por eso estos salen más caros que cualquier otro error de la lista.
examples: "We will eventually need SSO" is a promise, not a maybe.
"The file has sensible data" tells your team the data is level-headed.
"I can't assist the meeting" tells them you can't help the meeting.

blocks.body_en: Read each line in both directions: what the English word really means, and what you should say for the Spanish one.
blocks.body_es: Leé cada línea en los dos sentidos: qué significa de verdad la palabra inglesa, y qué tenés que decir para la castellana.
examples: actually = en realidad · actualmente = currently, right now
eventually = tarde o temprano · eventualmente = possibly, maybe
assist = ayudar · asistir a = attend
realize = darse cuenta · realizar = carry out, run, do
sensible = sensato · sensible = sensitive
support = apoyar, dar soporte · soportar (aguantar) = put up with, stand
compromise = acuerdo con concesiones · compromiso = commitment
resume = retomar · resumir = summarize, recap
success = éxito · exit = salida
large = grande · largo = long
blocks.title_en: The eight that cost you money

blocks.body_en: In every pair both sentences are correct English. Only one of them is what you were trying to say.
blocks.body_es: En todos los pares las dos oraciones son inglés correcto. Sólo una es la que estabas tratando de decir.

pairs.a: We're currently running the import.
pairs.b: We're actually running the import.
pairs.difference_es: La primera dice "en este momento". La segunda dice "en realidad, sí lo estamos corriendo", y corrige algo que el otro creía. Si en un mail de estado escribís la segunda, el cliente entiende que le estás discutiendo una suposición.

pairs.a: That's a sensible approach.
pairs.b: That's a sensitive topic.
pairs.difference_es: "Sensible" en inglés es sensato, razonable. "Sensitive" es sensible o delicado. Están cruzadas, y el caso caro es "sensitive data": datos sensibles. Decir "sensible data" es decir que los datos son sensatos.

pairs.a: We reached a compromise on the date.
pairs.b: We made a commitment on the date.
pairs.difference_es: "Compromise" es que las dos partes cedieron algo. "Commitment" es el compromiso que asumís. Si el cliente escucha "compromise" donde vos querías decir "compromiso", entiende que le vas a pedir que ceda.

pairs.a: We'll eventually need SSO.
pairs.b: We might need SSO.
pairs.difference_es: "Eventually" es "tarde o temprano", y es un sí con fecha incierta. Para decir "eventualmente", que es un quizás, va "might" o "possibly". Escribir la primera en una propuesta es comprometer alcance.

blocks.title_en: The word you said and the word you meant

blocks.body_en: Seven sentences from real Slack messages. Each one is one word away from saying what you meant.
blocks.body_es: Siete oraciones de mensajes de Slack de verdad. A cada una le falta cambiar una sola palabra.
examples: I can't assist the planning meeting. ✗ → I can't attend the planning meeting.
That file has sensible data. ✗ → That file has sensitive data.
Actually we're running the import. ✗ → Currently we're running the import.
We realize an audit every quarter. ✗ → We run an audit every quarter.
Let me resume what we agreed. ✗ → Let me summarize what we agreed.
I can't support another meeting about this. ✗ → I can't stand another meeting about this.
It was a large meeting, almost two hours. ✗ → It was a long meeting, almost two hours.

blocks.body_en: The safe version of each one, ready to paste into Slack or say in a call.
blocks.body_es: La versión segura de cada una, lista para pegar en Slack o decir en una llamada.
examples: We're currently running the migration on staging.
Actually, the bug wasn't in the backend; it was CSS.
I can't attend the planning meeting, I'm with a client.
Could you assist me with the deploy on Friday?
Careful, that config has sensitive data in it.
Given the deadline, cutting scope is the sensible option.
We run a security audit every quarter.
Let me summarize what we agreed before we hang up.
We reached a compromise on the delivery date.
I didn't realize the cron was disabled until the report came in empty.

lessons.goal_en: Stop saying "actually" for actualmente and "sensible" for sensible.
lessons.title_en: Words that look like Spanish and aren't

blocks.body_en: In Spanish you can ask for something straight and it lands as efficient. The same sentence translated word for word into English lands as an order. The fix is not being vague: it's a handful of fixed openings that leave the other person room to say no. That room is what makes them say yes.
blocks.body_es: En castellano pedís de frente y suena eficiente. Esa misma oración traducida palabra por palabra al inglés suena a orden. La solución no es andar con vueltas: son un puñado de aperturas fijas que le dejan al otro lugar para decir que no. Ese lugar es justamente lo que hace que te digan que sí.
examples: Could you send us the credentials when you get a chance?
I was wondering if we could move the call to Thursday.
It might be worth adding a cache before we scale.
blocks.title_en: Being direct is not the same as being clear

blocks.body_en: Requests open with could, would or I was wondering if. Suggestions get softened with might, could or maybe, instead of must or have to. Disagreement starts by granting something, then turns: that's a fair point, but. Notice that the past forms (could, would) are the polite ones; they aren't talking about the past at all.
blocks.body_es: Los pedidos abren con could, would o I was wondering if. Las sugerencias se suavizan con might, could o maybe, en vez de must o have to. El desacuerdo arranca concediendo algo y después gira: "that's a fair point, but". Ojo con esto: las formas de pasado (could, would) son las corteses, y no hablan del pasado.
examples: Would you mind sharing the logs from that window?
We could start with the API and leave the UI for phase two.
That's a fair point, but it would push the launch to May.
I'm afraid that won't be possible this sprint.

blocks.body_en: Every pair says the same thing. The first one is what a Spanish sentence turns into; the second is what you'd send to a client you want to keep.
blocks.body_es: Los dos dicen lo mismo. El primero es en lo que se convierte la oración en castellano; el segundo es lo que le mandás a un cliente que querés conservar.

pairs.a: Send me the credentials today.
pairs.b: Could you send me the credentials today?
pairs.difference_es: El imperativo en inglés suena a orden incluso con "please". "Could you" convierte la orden en pedido y no te quita ni un gramo de claridad.

pairs.a: You have to test it on Safari.
pairs.b: It would be worth testing it on Safari.
pairs.difference_es: "You have to" le dice al cliente lo que tiene que hacer. La segunda pone la recomendación sobre la mesa y lo deja decidir, que es tu lugar real.

pairs.a: That's wrong.
pairs.b: I'm not sure that would work with the current schema.
pairs.difference_es: En un code review o una call, "that's wrong" cierra la conversación. La segunda dice exactamente lo mismo y deja al otro respondiendo con datos.

pairs.a: I need an answer before Friday.
pairs.b: It would really help if we could get an answer before Friday.
pairs.difference_es: La primera pone tu necesidad como obligación del otro. La segunda explica el efecto de la respuesta, y el pedido sigue estando igual de claro.

blocks.body_en: These are all grammatical. That's exactly why they're dangerous: nobody corrects you, they just find you abrupt.
blocks.body_es: Todas son gramaticales, y por eso son peligrosas: nadie te corrige, sólo te encuentran cortante.
examples: I need you to review my PR. ✗ blunt → Could you take a look at my PR?
Please send me the file. ✗ still an order → Would you mind sending me the file?
You must fix this. ✗ → This will need a fix before we can release.
I want to know if it's ready. ✗ → I was wondering if it's ready.
It's impossible. ✗ → I'm afraid that won't be possible this sprint.

blocks.body_en: Requests, pushback and bad news. These carry most client conversations, and none of them make you sound unsure of yourself.
blocks.body_es: Pedidos, pushback y malas noticias. Con estas manejás casi cualquier conversación con un cliente, y ninguna te hace sonar inseguro.
examples: Could you walk me through what you have in mind?
Would you mind if we pushed the demo to Thursday?
I was wondering whether you'd had a chance to look at the proposal.
It might be worth starting with the smaller scope.
I see where you're coming from, but that would delay the launch.
I'm afraid we can't fit that into this sprint, but we could plan it for the next one.
Just to make sure we're on the same page, you want the export first.
Happy to do that if we can move the deadline by a week.

lessons.goal_en: Ask a client for things and disagree with them without sounding blunt.

blocks.body_en: Roll out and roll back are opposites, and the only difference is one small word at the end. English at work runs on these pairs: set up, look into, push back, follow up. You already understand them when you read them; the jump is using them yourself instead of the formal Latin verb, because "investigate the issue" is correct but "look into it" is what people say.
blocks.body_es: "Roll out" y "roll back" son opuestos y lo único que cambia es la palabrita del final. El inglés del trabajo funciona con estos pares. Entenderlos ya los entendés; el salto es usarlos vos en vez del verbo formal de raíz latina: "investigate the issue" es correcto, pero lo que se dice es "look into it".
examples: We rolled out the new pricing page to 10% of users.
We rolled back the release after the error spike.
Can you look into the failing test before standup?

blocks.body_en: Some phrasal verbs split and some don't. With a separable one, a noun can go either side, but a pronoun has to sit in the middle: roll the release back, roll it back. With an inseparable one nothing splits: look into it. When you turn the verb into a noun it becomes one word: a rollback, the rollout.
blocks.body_es: Algunos phrasal verbs se separan y otros no. Si es separable, el sustantivo puede ir de los dos lados, pero el pronombre va sí o sí en el medio: "roll the release back", "roll it back". Si es inseparable, no se separa nunca: "look into it". Y cuando el verbo se vuelve sustantivo, se escribe junto: "a rollback", "the rollout".
examples: We rolled the release back. / We rolled it back.
Can you set the environment up? / Can you set it up?
I looked into the bug. / I looked into it.
The rollback took four minutes.

blocks.body_en: Each pair is one particle or one position away from the other, and each one means something a client would notice.
blocks.body_es: Cada par está a una partícula o a una posición del otro, y en todos los casos el cliente nota la diferencia.

pairs.a: We rolled out the fix this morning.
pairs.b: We rolled back the fix this morning.
pairs.difference_es: "Roll out" es sacarlo a producción; "roll back" es volver a la versión anterior. Decir uno por el otro cambia por completo lo que entendió el cliente.

pairs.a: Can you roll it back?
pairs.b: Can you roll back it?
pairs.difference_es: La primera es la única correcta. Con pronombre, el phrasal separable se parte sí o sí: "roll it back", nunca "roll back it".

pairs.a: I'll look into the timeout.
pairs.b: I'll look for the timeout.
pairs.difference_es: "Look into" es investigar algo que ya sabés que pasa. "Look for" es buscar algo perdido, y con un bug reportado suena a que no lo encontrás.

pairs.a: I'll follow up with the client tomorrow.
pairs.b: I'll follow the client tomorrow.
pairs.difference_es: "Follow up with someone" es retomar el tema pendiente. Sin "up" queda "seguir a alguien", que es lo que hacés en redes sociales.

blocks.body_en: The first two are word order, the rest are the particle going missing or turning up where it shouldn't.
blocks.body_es: Los dos primeros son de orden; el resto son la partícula que falta o que aparece donde no va.
examples: Can you roll back it? ✗ → Can you roll it back?
I'll look it into. ✗ → I'll look into it.
Let's come out with a name. ✗ → Let's come up with a name.
We need to make a rollback of the deploy. ✗ → We need to roll the deploy back.
I set up it yesterday. ✗ → I set it up yesterday.

blocks.body_en: These twelve cover most of a week: deploys, code review, clients and planning.
blocks.body_es: Con estas doce cubrís casi toda una semana: deploys, code review, clientes y planificación.
examples: We're rolling it out to 10% first.
Let's roll it back and look into it tomorrow.
I'll set up a call with them for Thursday.
I ran into a rate limit while importing the data.
Can you follow up with them about the credentials?
We came up with a workaround for now.
I had to push back on the deadline.
Let me walk you through what happened.
We're ramping up the load slowly.
I'll hand this over to Sofía before I leave.
Let's wrap up and pick it up on Monday.
I'll back up the database before we migrate.

lessons.goal_en: Say what you did to the deploy the way your team says it, particle and all.

blocks.body_en: There is no logic to find here, and that is good news: it means you can stop looking for one. "Depend" comes with "on" the way a function comes with its signature. Learn the word and the preposition as a single unit and you never have to decide again.
blocks.body_es: Acá no hay lógica que descubrir, y eso es una buena noticia: podés dejar de buscarla. "Depend" viene con su "on" pegado, como una función viene con su firma. Aprendé la palabra y la preposición como una sola unidad y no la tenés que decidir nunca más. El problema del castellano es que un solo "de" cubre depend on, responsible for, consist of y in charge of.
examples: The timeline depends on how many integrations you need.
Martina is responsible for the CI pipeline.
The design consists of three services and one queue.
Ana is in charge of the release this week.
blocks.title_en: The preposition belongs to the word, not to the idea

blocks.body_en: Verbs bring one, adjectives bring one, and so do some nouns. These are the ones that show up in a standup, a review or a client call.
blocks.body_es: Los verbos traen la suya, los adjetivos también, y algunos sustantivos igual. Estas son las que aparecen en una daily, en un review o en una llamada con un cliente.
examples: Verbs with on: depend on, rely on, focus on, insist on, work on, agree on a date.
Verbs with for: wait for, ask for, apologize for, look for, pay for, account for.
Verbs with to: listen to, talk to, belong to, reply to, contribute to.
Verbs with about: think about, worry about, complain about, talk about, care about.
Verbs with of and with: consist of, deal with, agree with someone.
Adjectives: responsible for, good at, interested in, aware of, familiar with, similar to, different from.
Nouns: in charge of, a solution to, an answer to, a reason for, the impact on, an increase in.
And one with nothing at all: discuss the scope, not discuss about the scope.
blocks.title_en: The ones you'll use this week

blocks.body_en: These pairs are not right-and-wrong. Both sentences exist, and swapping the preposition changes what you just told the client.
blocks.body_es: Estos pares no son correcto contra incorrecto. Las dos oraciones existen, y cambiar la preposición cambia lo que le acabás de decir al cliente.

pairs.a: The estimate is based on the integrations you listed.
pairs.b: The team is based in Córdoba.
pairs.difference_es: "Based on" es en qué se apoya algo. "Based in" es dónde está. Si decís "the estimate is based in the integrations", el cliente escucha una dirección postal donde no la hay.

pairs.a: We agreed with the client.
pairs.b: We agreed on a new date.
pairs.difference_es: "Agree with" va con la persona o con la opinión con la que coincidís. "Agree on" va con la cosa que quedó decidida. En castellano las dos son "estar de acuerdo", y por eso sale el calco "agree in".

pairs.a: I'm looking for the config file.
pairs.b: I'm looking into the timeout.
pairs.difference_es: "Look for" es buscar algo que no encontrás. "Look into" es investigar algo que ya sabés que pasa. Con un bug reportado, "I'm looking for the bug" suena a que estás perdido.

pairs.a: She's responsible for the pipeline.
pairs.b: She's in charge of the release.
pairs.difference_es: Las dos son "encargada de" en castellano y llevan preposiciones distintas. No hay regla: "responsible" trae "for" y "in charge" trae "of", y se aprenden así, en bloque.

blocks.title_en: Same word, other preposition, other meaning

blocks.body_en: Almost all of these are the Spanish preposition translated straight through. The "de" of Spanish is the single biggest source of them.
blocks.body_es: Casi todos son la preposición del castellano traducida derecho. El "de" es el que más errores genera de todos.
examples: It depends of the scope. ✗ → It depends on the scope.
I'm interested on the role. ✗ → I'm interested in the role.
He's responsible of QA. ✗ → He's responsible for QA.
The design consists in three services. ✗ → The design consists of three services.
I don't agree in that estimate. ✗ → I don't agree with that estimate.
We discussed about the scope. ✗ → We discussed the scope.
Let me think in it and I'll get back to you. ✗ → Let me think about it and I'll get back to you.

blocks.body_en: Whole phrases, preposition included. Say them enough times and the preposition stops being a decision.
blocks.body_es: Frases enteras, con la preposición adentro. Decilas las veces suficientes y la preposición deja de ser una decisión.
examples: That depends on how many integrations you need.
I'm responsible for the release this sprint.
We're waiting for the client to confirm the scope.
Let's focus on the checkout bug today.
This service relies on the cache being warm.
I'd like to discuss the reporting scope before we sign.
Let me think about it and I'll get back to you tomorrow.
I'm not familiar with their auth provider yet.
Who's in charge of the migration window?
The estimate is based on what you sent last week.
I'll reply to their security questionnaire today.
We need a solution to the rate limit before Friday.

lessons.goal_en: Say depend on, responsible for and interested in without stopping to translate "de".
lessons.title_en: The preposition each word brings with it

blocks.body_en: Nobody in a daily stops you to fix your pronunciation, so this error survives for years. Every regular past is written -ed, but it comes out in three different ways, and only one of them adds a syllable. Saying "push-ed" instead of "pusht" is the fastest way to sound like a beginner while using perfect grammar.
blocks.body_es: Es el error que nadie te corrige: en una daily el otro entiende igual y sigue. Todos los pasados regulares se escriben -ed, pero se dicen de tres formas, y sólo una suma una sílaba. Hay un caso peor, que sí trae malentendidos: "wanted" y "want it" suenan casi igual, así que si le metés una sílaba de más a cualquier verbo, el otro escucha otra cosa.
examples: I pushed the fix. (pusht)
I wanted the fix. (wan-tid)

blocks.body_en: The rule is not about spelling, it's about the last sound before the -ed. Say the verb without the ending and feel your throat. If it vibrates, the -ed is a /d/. If it doesn't, it's a /t/. And if that last sound is already a t or a d, then and only then it becomes /ɪd/ and adds a syllable.
blocks.body_es: No mires cómo se escribe: escuchá el último sonido antes de la -ed. Poné la mano en la garganta y decí el verbo solo. Si vibra, va /d/. Si no vibra, va /t/. Y si ese último sonido ya es t o d, ahí sí suma una sílaba entera y suena /ɪd/.
examples: push (no vibration) → pushed = pusht
log (vibration) → logged = logd
start (already a t) → started = star-tid
need (already a d) → needed = ni-did
blocks.title_en: Put your hand on your throat

blocks.body_en: Say each pair out loud and count the syllables on your fingers. The spelling is almost identical; what comes out of your mouth isn't.
blocks.body_es: Decí cada par en voz alta y contá las sílabas con los dedos. Se escriben casi igual y suenan distinto. Ese es el ejercicio: notar el cambio antes de hablar.

pairs.a: I pushed the fix. (pusht, one syllable)
pairs.b: I posted the fix. (pous-tid, two syllables)
pairs.difference_es: Push termina en un sonido sordo, así que la -ed se pega como una t seca. Post ya termina en t, y ahí no te queda otra que abrir la boca y sumar la sílaba.

pairs.a: We released it on Friday. (rilist)
pairs.b: We used it on Friday. (iusd)
pairs.difference_es: Los dos se escriben con -sed, pero en release la s es sorda y da /t/, y en use esa s suena z, que vibra, y da /d/. Por eso la escritura no sirve de guía.

pairs.a: I liked the approach. (laikt)
pairs.b: I landed the client. (lan-did)
pairs.difference_es: La e escrita de "like" no se pronuncia, así que el último sonido es la k y sale /t/. En "land" el último sonido es d, y ahí sí suma sílaba.

pairs.a: The migration is finished. (finisht)
pairs.b: The team is dedicated. (de-di-quei-tid)
pairs.difference_es: La regla también vale para los adjetivos terminados en -ed, que son los que más aparecen en un standup.

blocks.body_en: Almost every mistake here is the same one: giving the -ed a syllable of its own, the way Spanish would. Only verbs ending in t or d get that.
blocks.body_es: Casi todos los errores son el mismo: darle a la -ed una sílaba propia, como haría el castellano. Sólo se la ganan los verbos que terminan en t o en d.
examples: I push-ed the fix. ✗ → I pushed (pusht) the fix. One syllable, not two.
We work-ed on it all week. ✗ → We worked (werkt) on it all week.
The build fail-ed. ✗ → The build failed (feild). Just a d, no syllable.
I lik-ed the approach. ✗ → I liked (laikt) the approach. The e is silent.
I want-ed to ship it. ✓ Here the syllable is real: wan-tid.

blocks.body_en: Standup lines with the pronunciation written next to each verb. Say them until the ending stops needing a decision.
blocks.body_es: Frases de daily con la pronunciación al lado de cada verbo. Decilas en voz alta hasta que la terminación te salga sin pensarla.
examples: I pushed (pusht) the fix and updated (up-dei-tid) the ticket.
We deployed (diploid) it last night and nothing failed (feild).
I checked (chekt) the logs and added (a-did) a retry.
The client asked (askt) for it, so we started (star-tid) yesterday.
I finished (finisht) the review and merged (merjd) it this morning.

lessons.goal_en: Say any regular past without adding a syllable that isn't there.

blocks.body_en: In a standup, a retro or a handover you spend more time saying what someone else said than saying your own opinion. English moves the tenses one step back when you do that, because you're telling it from further away. Get that step right and the story is easy to follow; get it wrong and people can't tell what's still true.
blocks.body_es: En una daily, una retro o un traspaso pasás más tiempo contando lo que dijo otro que dando tu opinión. Cuando hacés eso, el inglés corre los tiempos un paso para atrás, porque lo contás desde más lejos. Si acertás ese paso, la historia se sigue sola; si no, nadie sabe qué sigue vigente.
examples: The client said they needed it by Friday.
Diego told me he had already fixed it.
They asked whether we could add SSO before launch.
blocks.title_en: Half of a lead's English is other people's words

blocks.body_en: Present goes to past, past goes to past perfect, will goes to would and can goes to could. Time words move too: tomorrow becomes the next day. And the two verbs are not interchangeable: you tell someone something, but you say something, with no person after it.
blocks.body_es: El presente pasa a pasado, el pasado a past perfect, will a would y can a could. Las marcas de tiempo también se corren: "tomorrow" se vuelve "the next day". Y ojo con los dos verbos, que no son intercambiables: "tell" lleva persona ("tell me"), "say" no ("say that...").
examples: "We need it by Friday" → They said they needed it by Friday.
"I've deployed it" → She said she had deployed it.
"I'll send it tomorrow" → He said he would send it the next day.
"Can you review it?" → She asked me if I could review it.
blocks.title_en: One step back, and two words to watch

blocks.body_en: Backshift is the default, not a law. If what was said is still true right now, plenty of speakers leave the tense alone. The other pairs are the two mistakes that actually change the meaning.
blocks.body_es: Correr el tiempo es lo normal, pero no es una ley. Si lo que se dijo sigue siendo cierto ahora, se puede dejar el presente. Los otros pares son los dos errores que sí cambian el significado.

pairs.a: She said the API needs an auth header.
pairs.b: She said the API needed an auth header.
pairs.difference_es: La primera deja el presente porque la API sigue necesitando el header hoy. La segunda suena a que era así en ese momento y capaz ya cambió.

pairs.a: He said me it was ready.
pairs.b: He told me it was ready.
pairs.difference_es: "Say" no lleva persona directa. Con "me" va "told". Es el error más frecuente y se escucha enseguida.

pairs.a: She asked me where the file was.
pairs.b: She asked me where was the file.
pairs.difference_es: La primera es la correcta. Al reportar una pregunta, el orden vuelve a ser de afirmación: sujeto y después verbo.

pairs.a: The client said they will sign on Monday.
pairs.b: The client said they would sign on Monday, and they did.
pairs.difference_es: Si el lunes ya pasó, dejar "will" suena a promesa todavía abierta. Con "would" queda claro que lo contás desde después.

blocks.title_en: When the step back happens, and when it doesn't

blocks.body_en: The first three come from Spanish using one verb where English uses two, or keeping the question word order.
blocks.body_es: Los tres primeros salen de que el castellano usa un verbo donde el inglés usa dos, o de conservar el orden de pregunta.
examples: He said me the deploy failed. ✗ → He told me the deploy failed.
She told that it was ready. ✗ → She said that it was ready.
They asked me what do I need. ✗ → They asked me what I needed.
He asked me if I can review it yesterday. ✗ → He asked me if I could review it.
She said me to send the invoice. ✗ → She asked me to send the invoice.

blocks.body_en: Standup, retro and handover. These are the frames you drop other people's words into.
blocks.body_es: Daily, retro y traspaso. Son los moldes donde metés las palabras de los demás.
examples: The client said they'd get back to us by Wednesday.
Laura mentioned that the staging data was out of date.
They asked if we could demo it before the end of the month.
He told me he was blocked on the credentials.
Just to relay what they said, the priority is the export screen.
She suggested we start with the API.
According to the client, the deadline hasn't moved.

lessons.goal_en: Relay what the client asked for, in a standup or a retro, without losing the thread.

blocks.body_en: "We'll migrate the users by Friday" leaves a small door open: maybe you're still migrating on Friday. "By Friday we'll have migrated the users" closes it: stand on Friday, look back, it's done. That's what an estimate needs to sound like, and it's one word away.
blocks.body_es: "We'll migrate by Friday" deja una puertita abierta: capaz el viernes todavía estás migrando. "By Friday we'll have migrated" la cierra: te parás el viernes, mirás para atrás y está hecho. Es la diferencia entre una intención y un compromiso, y te cuesta una palabra.
examples: By Friday we'll have migrated all the users.
This time tomorrow I'll be running the workshop.
blocks.title_en: Standing in the future, looking back

blocks.body_en: Will have + participle for something finished before a future point. Will be + -ing for something in progress at that point. Will have been + -ing when you want to say how long it will have lasted. The time marker usually comes first: by Friday, by the time you're back, this time tomorrow.
blocks.body_es: Will have + participio: terminado antes de ese momento. Will be + -ing: en curso en ese momento. Will have been + -ing: cuánto tiempo va a llevar al llegar ahí. Casi siempre arranca con la marca de tiempo: by Friday, by the time you're back, this time tomorrow.
examples: By the end of the sprint we'll have closed the top three bugs.
I'll be working from the client's office on Tuesday.
By the launch we'll have been testing this for six months.
By then the deploy will already be done.

blocks.body_en: Each pair points at the same Friday. What changes is whether the work is done, still running, or simply happening at some point.
blocks.body_es: Cada par apunta al mismo viernes. Lo que cambia es si el trabajo está terminado, todavía en curso, o simplemente ocurre en algún momento. Es lo que un cliente escucha cuando le das una fecha.

pairs.a: By Friday we'll migrate the users.
pairs.b: By Friday we'll have migrated the users.
pairs.difference_es: La forma con "will have" garantiza que el viernes ya está hecho. La otra deja lugar a que el viernes sea el día en que recién lo estás haciendo.

pairs.a: Tomorrow at 10 I'll run the workshop.
pairs.b: Tomorrow at 10 I'll be running the workshop.
pairs.difference_es: Con "will run" contás el hecho entero: mañana das el taller. Con "will be running" te ubicás adentro de ese momento, y por eso sirve para avisar que no vas a poder contestar.

pairs.a: By June we'll have tested it with three clients.
pairs.b: By June we'll have been testing it for six months.
pairs.difference_es: La primera cuenta resultados terminados: tres clientes. La segunda cuenta tiempo acumulado: seis meses probando. Una muestra avance, la otra muestra esfuerzo sostenido.

pairs.a: I'll work on the API next week.
pairs.b: I'll be working on the API next week.
pairs.difference_es: "I'll work" suena a decisión que tomás ahora. "I'll be working" suena a plan que ya está en marcha, y por eso queda más suave cuando avisás en qué vas a estar.

blocks.title_en: Finished, in progress, or just later

blocks.body_en: Two of these break the shape itself; the other two are the Spanish sentence coming through untranslated.
blocks.body_es: Dos rompen la estructura y dos son el castellano pasando de largo. La de "will have been migrated" es la más cara: esa es pasiva y significa que alguien más los migró.
examples: By noon I will have finish the report. ✗ → By noon I will have finished the report.
By Friday we will finished the migration. ✗ → By Friday we will have finished the migration.
By the time you come back, I will finish it. ✗ → By the time you come back, I'll have finished it.
By Friday we will have been migrated the users. ✗ (eso es pasiva) → By Friday we will have migrated the users.

blocks.body_en: Estimates, handovers and status updates. These are the lines that make a date sound like a commitment.
blocks.body_es: Estimaciones, entregas y reportes de avance. Son las frases que hacen que una fecha suene a compromiso y no a deseo.
examples: By the time you're back on Monday, we'll have finished the migration.
I'll be in workshops all Tuesday, so I'll answer in the evening.
By the end of the quarter we'll have onboarded every team.
We'll have a first version ready by Thursday, and I'll walk you through it.
By then we'll have been running it in production for a month.

lessons.goal_en: Give a client a deadline that sounds finished, not hopeful.

blocks.body_en: Most of the future you talk about at work is not a prediction: it's an agenda. The demo is at ten, you're deploying on Thursday, the client is flying in on Monday. English says those in the present, because they're already settled. Using "will" there makes it sound like you just thought of it.
blocks.body_es: Casi todo el futuro del trabajo no es una predicción: es agenda. La demo es a las diez, deployás el jueves, el cliente llega el lunes. El inglés eso lo dice en presente, porque ya está arreglado. Si metés "will", suena a que lo estás decidiendo recién ahora, y con un cliente eso resta.
examples: We're deploying on Thursday, so let's freeze on Wednesday.
The retro is at 3 your time.

blocks.body_en: Present continuous for personal arrangements you've already made. Present simple for timetables: flights, meetings, opening hours. And present simple again after when, as soon as, until, before and after, where "will" is simply not allowed.
blocks.body_es: Presente continuo para planes que ya arreglaste. Presente simple para horarios fijos (vuelos, reuniones, agenda). Y presente simple otra vez después de when, as soon as, until, before y after, donde "will" no entra: el futuro ya lo marca la otra mitad de la oración.
examples: I'm meeting the client on Tuesday.
The standup starts at 9:30.
I'll ping you as soon as the build finishes.
Let's not merge until the client approves the designs.

blocks.body_en: All of these are correct English. What changes is how settled the plan sounds, and that's exactly what a client hears.
blocks.body_es: Todas son correctas. Lo que cambia es qué tan cerrado suena el plan, y eso es justo lo que escucha el cliente. Leelas pensando en una reunión de seguimiento.

pairs.a: We're deploying on Thursday.
pairs.b: We'll deploy on Thursday.
pairs.difference_es: El continuo dice que ya está agendado, con la gente reservada. Con "will" suena a decisión tomada en el momento, y a que todavía puede moverse.

pairs.a: The demo is at 10.
pairs.b: The demo will be at 10.
pairs.difference_es: El presente simple lo trata como horario fijo, igual que un vuelo. Con "will" suena a que estás anunciando algo que recién se define.

pairs.a: I'm meeting the client on Tuesday.
pairs.b: I meet the client every Tuesday.
pairs.difference_es: El continuo es una cita puntual que ya tenés arreglada. El simple, con "every", es tu rutina: pasa todas las semanas.

pairs.a: I'll call you when the tests finish.
pairs.b: I'll call you when the tests are finished.
pairs.difference_es: Las dos andan y en ninguna entra "will" después de "when". La segunda pone un poco más de foco en el estado final, en que ya estén terminados.

blocks.title_en: Arranged, scheduled, or decided right now

blocks.body_en: The first two are the same mistake wearing different clothes: "will" after a time word. The others come from Spanish using the plain present where English needs the continuous.
blocks.body_es: Los dos primeros son el mismo error: "will" después de una palabra de tiempo. Los otros vienen de que en castellano usás el presente pelado ("mañana viajo") donde el inglés pide el continuo.
examples: I'll ping you when the build will finish. ✗ → I'll ping you when the build finishes.
Let's wait until the client will answer. ✗ → Let's wait until the client answers.
Tomorrow I travel to the client's office. ✗ → Tomorrow I'm travelling to the client's office.
What do you do this weekend? ✗ (si preguntás por planes) → What are you doing this weekend?

blocks.body_en: Five lines for scheduling, handovers and the end of the day.
blocks.body_es: Cinco frases para agendar, avisar y cerrar el día. Son de las que más vas a usar por Slack.
examples: I'm heading out at 5, but I'm online again after dinner.
We're releasing on Thursday, so let's freeze the branch on Wednesday.
What time does your flight land?
I'll send the recording as soon as the call ends.
I'm off on Friday — Ana is covering the deploy.

lessons.goal_en: Talk about what's already in the calendar without sounding like you're deciding it on the spot.

blocks.body_en: Every incident story has two layers. One is what was already running: the deploy, the review, the call. The other is the thing that cut in: the alert, the crash, the message. Past continuous paints the first layer, past simple fires the second. Get this right and your postmortem tells itself.
blocks.body_es: En castellano decís "estaba deployando cuando saltó la alerta" sin pensarlo, porque tenés las dos formas. En inglés son las mismas dos capas: el fondo va en pasado continuo (was/were + -ing) y el golpe que lo interrumpe va en pasado simple. Si ponés las dos en simple, la historia pierde el orden.
examples: I was reviewing the PR when the alert fired.
We were deploying to staging and everything looked fine.

blocks.body_en: Past continuous is was or were plus the -ing form: I was, he was, we were, they were. Past simple is the second column of the verb: fired, crashed, went, broke. "While" almost always introduces the background; "when" usually introduces the interruption.
blocks.body_es: Pasado continuo: was o were + -ing. Pasado simple: la segunda columna del verbo, que para los irregulares te la da el glosario. Regla práctica: lo que va después de "while" suele ser el fondo, y lo que va después de "when" suele ser el corte.
examples: I was debugging the queue when the pager went off.
While we were waiting for the client, the build finished.
The dashboard was showing stale data all morning.
She called me twice before I noticed.

blocks.body_en: Both sides of each pair are correct English. What changes is the order of events and whether the action was finished.
blocks.body_es: Los dos lados son correctos. Lo que cambia es el orden de los hechos y si la acción llegó a terminar. Leelos en voz alta: en una reunión, elegir mal te hace contar otra historia.

pairs.a: I was reviewing the PR when the alert fired.
pairs.b: I reviewed the PR when the alert fired.
pairs.difference_es: Con "was reviewing" estabas en el medio de la revisión y la alerta te cortó. Con "reviewed" la alerta vino primero y después revisaste, como si fuera tu reacción.

pairs.a: When the client called, we were deploying.
pairs.b: When the client called, we deployed.
pairs.difference_es: Con el continuo, el deploy ya venía corriendo cuando sonó el teléfono. Con el simple, el deploy arrancó después de la llamada: suena a que lo hiciste porque te llamaron.

pairs.a: The API was returning 500s all morning.
pairs.b: The API returned 500s twice.
pairs.difference_es: El continuo estira el problema en el tiempo: toda la mañana así. El simple cuenta eventos cerrados, que podés numerar. Para un cliente, la diferencia entre "estuvo caído" y "falló dos veces" es enorme.

pairs.a: I was talking to Ana about the estimate.
pairs.b: I talked to Ana about the estimate.
pairs.difference_es: El continuo suena a conversación en curso, y muchas veces a que quedó por la mitad. El simple la da por terminada: hablaste y listo, hay una conclusión.

blocks.body_en: Three of these come from translating word by word, and the fourth from verbs that simply refuse the -ing form.
blocks.body_es: Tres salen de traducir literal y el cuarto es una familia de verbos que no admite -ing: los de estado (know, want, need, mean, seem, belong).
examples: While I deployed, the disk filled up. ✗ → While I was deploying, the disk filled up.
I was reviewing the PR and I was finding the bug. ✗ → I was reviewing the PR and I found the bug.
What were you doing yesterday at the retro? ✗ (si querés el hecho) → What did you do at the retro?
I was knowing about the outage. ✗ → I knew about the outage.

blocks.body_en: These five carry a whole incident story. Learn them whole and the tenses come along for free.
blocks.body_es: Con estas cinco contás un incidente entero. Aprendelas como bloque: el tiempo verbal viene adentro y no lo tenés que armar bajo presión.
examples: I was just looking at that when you pinged me.
We were halfway through the deploy when the alert fired.
While the team was investigating, I kept the client updated.
It was working fine until we changed the config.
Sorry, I was on a call — what did I miss?

lessons.goal_en: Tell an incident story where it's clear what was already happening and what suddenly hit.

blocks.body_en: A postmortem is never one straight line. There's the moment you noticed, and there's everything that had already happened before you noticed. Past perfect is the flashback: it takes one action and pushes it behind the rest of the story, so nobody has to guess the order.
blocks.body_es: Es el "ya había pasado" del castellano. En un postmortem hay dos momentos: cuando te diste cuenta, y todo lo que pasó antes. El past perfect empuja una acción hacia atrás para que quede claro qué vino primero, sin que el otro tenga que reconstruirlo solo.
examples: When we noticed, the job had already deleted half the records.
The client had approved the scope before we started.

blocks.body_en: Had plus the past participle, for every person: I had, she had, they had. In speech it's almost always contracted to 'd, and that's where it gets hard to hear: "he'd pushed" is "he had pushed". The negative is hadn't.
blocks.body_es: Had + participio, igual para todas las personas. Al hablar casi siempre va contraído: "he'd pushed" es "he had pushed", no "he would push". Esa contracción es la que se te va a escapar escuchando, así que vale la pena decirla en voz alta unas cuantas veces.
examples: I'd already merged it when you left the comment.
They hadn't tested it on Safari.
By Monday the team had closed every blocker.
Had you seen the logs before the call?

blocks.body_en: Both sides are correct English. The past perfect version moves one action behind the other; the simple version lines them up in order.
blocks.body_es: Los dos lados son correctos. Con past perfect, una acción se va atrás en el tiempo; con pasado simple, las dos quedan en fila, una después de la otra. Fijate cómo cambia quién hizo qué primero.

pairs.a: When I joined, they migrated to Kubernetes.
pairs.b: When I joined, they had migrated to Kubernetes.
pairs.difference_es: Sin "had", la migración pasó después de que entraste, como si tu llegada la hubiera disparado. Con "had", ya estaba hecha y vos la encontraste funcionando.

pairs.a: When the client called, we fixed the issue.
pairs.b: When the client called, we had fixed the issue.
pairs.difference_es: Sin "had" quedás como el equipo que reacciona al reclamo. Con "had" el arreglo ya estaba, y la llamada te encontró tranquilo. En una reunión con cliente es la diferencia entre ir atrás o ir adelante.

pairs.a: She said she fixed it.
pairs.b: She said she had fixed it.
pairs.difference_es: Sin "had" suena a que lo arregló más o menos en ese momento. Con "had" queda claro que ya estaba arreglado antes de que lo dijera: es lo natural cuando reportás lo que alguien te contó.

pairs.a: He left before I called him.
pairs.b: He had left before I called him.
pairs.difference_es: Acá las dos dicen lo mismo, porque "before" ya ordena los hechos. La versión con "had" sólo subraya que cuando llamaste ya no estaba. Con before y after, el past perfect es opcional.

blocks.body_en: The big one is mixing "have" into a story that lives entirely in the past. The other is using the flashback when there's nothing to flash back to.
blocks.body_es: El error grande es meter "have" en una historia que pasa toda en el pasado. El otro es usar el flashback cuando no hay dos momentos: si la historia avanza derecho, va pasado simple.
examples: When I joined, they have already migrated. ✗ → When I joined, they had already migrated.
Yesterday I had deployed the fix. ✗ (no hay segundo momento) → Yesterday I deployed the fix.
I had went through the logs. ✗ → I had gone through the logs.
After the alert had fired, I had opened the dashboard. ✗ → After the alert fired, I opened the dashboard.

blocks.body_en: Postmortem and interview lines. Each one puts an earlier action where it belongs.
