blocks.body_es: Frases de postmortem y de entrevista. Cada una ubica una acción anterior en su lugar, que es justo lo que te piden cuando contás un problema.
examples: By the time we noticed, the queue had already backed up.
I hadn't seen that error before, so it took me a while.
We had tested it locally, but not with production data.
The client had signed off on the scope, so we kept going.
I realized I'd pushed to the wrong branch.

lessons.goal_en: Explain what had already gone wrong before the moment your story starts.

blocks.body_en: Some things are not finished and not new: the outage that started this morning, the integration you picked up three weeks ago, the job you have had since 2021. English has one tense for exactly that stretch, and it is the one Spanish speakers skip.
blocks.body_es: Hay cosas que no terminaron ni son nuevas: el incidente que arrancó a la mañana, la integración que agarraste hace tres semanas, el trabajo que tenés desde 2021. El inglés tiene un tiempo para ese tramo entre el arranque y el ahora, y es el que los hispanohablantes se saltean, porque en castellano alcanza con el presente.
examples: I've been working on the payments integration for three weeks.
We've been getting timeouts since the deploy.
blocks.title_en: The line from then to now

blocks.body_en: Have or has been plus the -ing form. Use "for" with a length of time and "since" with the point it started. To ask, put "How long" in front: it is the single most useful question in a one-on-one.
blocks.body_es: Have o has been + -ing. "For" va con cuánto tiempo (for three weeks, for two days) y "since" con desde cuándo (since March, since the deploy). Para preguntar, "How long" adelante. Regla rápida: si podés contestar "desde", usás since; si contestás "hace tanto", usás for.
examples: I've been reviewing PRs all morning.
The client has been waiting for an answer since Tuesday.
How long have you been working on the payments integration?
We've been seeing this error for about two days.
blocks.title_en: have been plus -ing, with for or since

blocks.body_en: The continuous points at the activity and how long it has been running. The simple perfect points at the finished result. Pick the one that matches what you actually mean.
blocks.body_es: El continuo apunta a la actividad y a cuánto lleva corriendo; el perfecto simple apunta al resultado terminado. En una daily casi siempre querés el continuo, porque estás contando en qué andás, no qué cerraste.

pairs.a: I've been fixing the flaky test.
pairs.b: I've fixed the flaky test.
pairs.difference_es: La primera dice en qué estuviste metido y deja abierto si terminaste. La segunda dice que está listo. Si la decís en una daily sin querer, tu lead va a pensar que el test ya anda.

pairs.a: We've been talking to three candidates.
pairs.b: We've talked to three candidates.
pairs.difference_es: La primera pinta un proceso abierto, todavía sin decisión. La segunda suena a cuenta cerrada: tres entrevistas hechas, y ahora se decide.

pairs.a: I've been working here since 2021.
pairs.b: I worked here in 2021.
pairs.difference_es: La primera te ubica hoy en ese trabajo, con cuatro años encima. La segunda te saca de ahí: suena a que ya no estás. Es el error que más caro sale en una entrevista.

pairs.a: How long have you been working on it?
pairs.b: How long did it take you?
pairs.difference_es: La primera pregunta por algo que sigue en curso. La segunda pregunta por algo que ya terminó y quiere saber cuánto llevó en total.

blocks.body_en: In Spanish the present tense covers all of this, so the present tense is what comes out first. It is the fastest way to sound like a translation.
blocks.body_es: En castellano el presente cubre todo esto ("trabajo acá desde 2021", "hace dos semanas que esperamos"), así que el presente es lo primero que sale. Es el calco que más rápido te delata.
examples: I work here since 2021. ✗ → I've been working here since 2021.
We are waiting for the client for two weeks. ✗ → We've been waiting for the client for two weeks.
How long are you debugging it? ✗ → How long have you been debugging it?
I am knowing him since the bootcamp. ✗ → I've known him since the bootcamp. (know no admite continuo)

blocks.body_en: Status updates live here. These five cover most of what you need to say about something that is still in progress.
blocks.body_es: Los updates de estado viven acá. Con estas cinco cubrís casi todo lo que tenés que decir sobre algo que todavía está en curso.
examples: I've been looking into it since this morning, and I'm close.
We've been seeing this intermittently for a couple of days.
How long has it been happening on your side?
I've been meaning to ask you about that.
They've been pushing for a demo since last week.

lessons.goal_en: Say how long something has been going on, and ask someone else, without sounding like a translation.

blocks.body_en: When you tell a client or your team where things stand, you are not telling a story with dates. You are saying what is true now because of something you did. That is the present perfect, and it is the tense that carries most of a standup.
blocks.body_es: En castellano decís "ya lo arreglé" y "lo arreglé ayer" con el mismo tiempo, así que no tenés que elegir. En inglés sí: si mencionás cuándo pasó, va past simple; si lo que importa es cómo está la cosa ahora, va present perfect. No es una regla de cortesía ni de formalidad: cambia de qué estás hablando.
examples: I've fixed the flaky test, so the pipeline is green again.
We've added SSO, so your team can log in with Google.
blocks.title_en: The tense that reports instead of narrating

blocks.body_en: Have or has plus the past participle. In speech it is almost always contracted, and that contraction is where most of the listening trouble lives: "she's pushed" is "she has pushed", not "she is pushed".
blocks.body_es: Have o has + participio. Al hablar casi siempre va contraído, y ahí está la trampa para escuchar: "she's pushed" es "she has pushed", no "she is pushed". Con los verbos irregulares, el participio es la tercera columna: go → went → gone. El glosario te la resuelve en dos segundos.
examples: She's pushed the fix to staging.
We haven't heard back from the client yet.
Have you deployed it to production?
I've never worked with Kafka at this scale.
blocks.title_en: have or has, plus the participle

blocks.body_en: Each pair is true. What changes is what you are pointing at: the result you have now, or the moment it happened.
blocks.body_es: Los dos lados de cada par son correctos. Lo que cambia es a qué apuntás: al resultado que tenés ahora, o al momento en que pasó. Leelos en voz alta y fijate cuál dirías en una daily y cuál en un postmortem.

pairs.a: I've fixed the login bug.
pairs.b: I fixed the login bug yesterday.
pairs.difference_es: La primera reporta el estado: hoy el login anda. La segunda cuenta cuándo lo arreglaste, y por eso necesita ese "yesterday" para no quedar coja.

pairs.a: We've worked with three fintechs.
pairs.b: We worked with three fintechs in 2023.
pairs.difference_es: La primera es tu experiencia acumulada hasta hoy, la que usarías para ganar un cliente. La segunda encierra todo en un año cerrado, como si eso ya fuera parte del pasado.

pairs.a: Have you talked to the client?
pairs.b: Did you talk to the client this morning?
pairs.difference_es: La primera pregunta si pasó en algún momento hasta ahora, sin importar cuándo. La segunda pregunta por un rato que ya terminó, y por eso pide past simple.

pairs.a: The API has gone down twice.
pairs.b: The API went down twice last night.
pairs.difference_es: La primera deja la cuenta abierta: puede volver a caerse hoy. La segunda cierra el episodio en anoche, que es lo que querés en un postmortem.

blocks.title_en: The same fact, two different points

blocks.body_en: Almost every mistake here comes from the same place: Spanish lets you use the perfect with a finished time, and English does not.
blocks.body_es: Casi todos los errores salen del mismo lugar: en castellano podés decir "lo he hecho ayer" y se entiende, en inglés no. Si en la oración aparece un momento terminado, el present perfect queda descartado.
examples: I've talked to the client last Friday. ✗ → I talked to the client last Friday.
I've finished it ten minutes ago. ✗ → I finished it ten minutes ago. (ago siempre cierra el tiempo)
When have you deployed it? ✗ → When did you deploy it? (when pregunta por un momento)
I have went through the logs. ✗ → I have gone through the logs.

blocks.body_en: Five blocks you can drop into a standup or a call today. Learn them whole and the grammar comes along for free.
blocks.body_es: Cinco bloques para usar mañana en una daily o una call. Aprendelos enteros: la gramática viene adentro y no la tenés que armar en el momento.
examples: I've just pushed a fix, can you pull before you test?
We've already covered that in the RFC, let me send you the link.
I haven't had a chance to review it yet.
Have you seen anything weird in the logs since the release?
I've worked on similar integrations before, so I know where this usually breaks.

lessons.goal_en: Report where things stand right now, and back yourself with experience, without giving dates.
lessons.title_en: Present perfect for results and experience

blocks.body_en: Spanish does everything with "hacer". English splits the job in two. You make something that did not exist before you spoke: a decision, a change, a mistake, progress, an offer. You do something that was already on the list: a review, some research, the testing, the documentation. And a handful of Spanish "hacer" phrases use neither verb at all.
blocks.body_es: El castellano resuelve todo con "hacer". El inglés lo parte en dos. Con make producís algo que antes no existía: a decision, a change, a mistake, progress. Con do ejecutás algo que ya estaba en la lista: a review, some research, the testing. Y hay un puñado de "hacer" que en inglés no usan ni uno ni otro.
examples: We made a change to the schema on Tuesday.
Can you do a quick review before lunch?
I made a mistake in the migration script.
Someone has to do some research on their API first.
blocks.title_en: One verb in Spanish, two in English

blocks.body_en: The general idea helps, but the pairs are fixed. Learn them as pairs, the way you learn a library's method names.
blocks.body_es: La idea general ayuda, pero los pares son fijos. Aprendelos de a par, como aprendés los nombres de los métodos de una librería.
examples: make: a decision, a mistake, progress, a change, an offer, an exception, a suggestion, sure, sense, a difference, an effort, a plan.
do: a review, some research, the testing, the documentation, a demo, a favour, business, your best, a pass over something.
neither: ask a question, take a photo, give a talk, run an audit, have a meeting.
Just to make sure I got it right, the report runs every Monday?
That retry loop doesn't make much sense to me.
Could you do me a favour and review this before you log off?
blocks.title_en: The pairs you'll need this week

blocks.body_en: The first two pairs are both correct and mean different things. The last two are the sentence you want next to the sentence a Spanish speaker actually says.
blocks.body_es: Los dos primeros pares están bien los dos y significan cosas distintas. Los dos últimos ponen al lado la oración que querías decir y la que realmente dice un hispanohablante.

pairs.a: We made a change to the schema.
pairs.b: We did a full review of the schema.
pairs.difference_es: El cambio no existía antes: lo producís, así que va make. El review es una tarea que estaba en la lista y la ejecutás, así que va do. Es la diferencia entre crear y correr algo que ya estaba definido.

pairs.a: He made the call to roll back.
pairs.b: He made a call to the client.
pairs.difference_es: "Make the call" con "the" es tomar la decisión, la que alguien tiene que bancarse. "Make a call" con "a" es levantar el teléfono. En un postmortem la diferencia entre las dos es quién decidió qué.

pairs.a: Can you do a quick review before lunch?
pairs.b: Can you make a quick review before lunch?
pairs.difference_es: La segunda es el calco directo de "hacer un review" y no la dice ningún nativo. Un review es tarea, y las tareas van con do.

pairs.a: Can I ask a question about the deploy?
pairs.b: Can I make a question about the deploy?
pairs.difference_es: Acá no ganan ni make ni do: "hacer una pregunta" en inglés es "ask a question". Es el error que más rápido te delata en una daily, porque las preguntas se hacen todos los días.

blocks.body_en: Six sentences you have probably said out loud. All six are one verb away from being right.
blocks.body_es: Seis oraciones que seguro dijiste en voz alta. A las seis les falta cambiar un solo verbo.
examples: I did a mistake in the migration. ✗ → I made a mistake in the migration.
We made a code review yesterday. ✗ → We did a code review yesterday.
Can I make a question? ✗ → Can I ask a question?
It doesn't do sense to me. ✗ → It doesn't make sense to me.
Let's do a decision before Friday. ✗ → Let's make a decision before Friday.
We did a lot of progress this week. ✗ → We made a lot of progress this week.

blocks.body_en: Ten whole phrases. Say the phrase, not the verb plus the noun, and you stop choosing.
blocks.body_es: Diez frases enteras. Decí la frase, no el verbo más el sustantivo, y dejás de tener que elegir.
examples: We made good progress on the importer this week.
Just to make sure, the report runs every Monday?
That doesn't make sense to me, can you walk me through it?
Sorry, I made a mistake in the migration script.
We can make an exception this time, but not in phase two.
Somebody has to make the call on this.
Can you do a quick review before you log off?
We do a round of manual testing before every release.
I'll do some research on their API and come back with a number.
Can I ask a question about the deploy window?

lessons.goal_en: Pick between the two English verbs hiding behind "hacer" without stopping to think.

blocks.body_en: In Spanish the person who hears you is an extra pronoun you can drop anywhere: "me dijo", "le dije", "nos dijo". In English that person is what decides the verb. If the listener sits right after the verb, it has to be tell. If there is no listener, it has to be say. That is the whole decision, and you can make it before you finish the sentence.
blocks.body_es: En castellano la persona que te escucha es un pronombre suelto que ponés donde quieras: me dijo, le dije, nos dijo. En inglés esa persona es lo que decide el verbo. Si la persona va pegada al verbo, es tell. Si no hay persona, es say. Eso es toda la decisión, y la podés tomar antes de terminar la oración.
examples: She told me the build was red.
She said the build was red.
They told us the budget is frozen.
They said to us that the budget is frozen.

blocks.body_en: Tell takes a person and then the message, or a person and then an instruction. Say takes the message, and if you want to name the listener you need "to" first. Then there are the frozen phrases, which ignore all of this and just have to be learned.
blocks.body_es: Tell lleva la persona y después el mensaje, o la persona y después una instrucción. Say lleva el mensaje, y si querés nombrar a quien escucha necesitás un "to" antes. Después están las frases congeladas, que se saltean todo esto y hay que aprenderlas de memoria.
examples: tell + person + message: She told me the deploy failed.
tell + person + to + verb: I told him to rerun the pipeline.
say + message: He said the invoice is approved.
say + to + person: He said to me that the invoice is approved.
always tell: tell the truth, tell a lie, tell the difference, tell a story.
always say: say hello, say sorry, say thank you, say a word.

blocks.body_en: The first pair is two correct sentences. The rest put the right sentence next to the one that comes out when you translate from Spanish.
blocks.body_es: El primer par son dos oraciones correctas. Los demás ponen al lado la oración buena y la que sale cuando traducís del castellano.

pairs.a: She told me the build was red.
pairs.b: She said the build was red.
pairs.difference_es: Las dos están bien. En la primera nombrás a quien escucha y por eso va tell; en la segunda no hay nadie escuchando en la oración y por eso va say. Decidís según si vas a nombrar a la persona o no.

pairs.a: They said to us that the budget is frozen.
pairs.b: They said us that the budget is frozen.
pairs.difference_es: Say puede nombrar a la persona, pero necesita "to" en el medio. Sin ese "to" la oración no existe en inglés, y "said us" es el calco exacto de "nos dijo". Lo más simple es cambiar el verbo y decir "told us".

pairs.a: Let's tell the truth about the estimate.
pairs.b: Let's say the truth about the estimate.
pairs.difference_es: "Tell the truth" es una frase congelada y no cambia aunque no haya persona. Pasa lo mismo con "tell a lie" y "tell the difference": son de tell, punto.

pairs.a: I just wanted to say thanks for covering my shift.
pairs.b: I just wanted to tell thanks for covering my shift.
pairs.difference_es: Del otro lado están las frases que son de say sin discusión: say thanks, say hello, say sorry. Tell necesita una persona y acá no la hay, así que no entra.

blocks.body_en: Six of them, and the first one is the single most common mistake a Spanish speaker makes in English at work.
blocks.body_es: Seis, y el primero es el error más frecuente que comete un hispanohablante en inglés en el trabajo.
examples: He said me the deploy failed. ✗ → He told me the deploy failed.
She told that the API is down. ✗ → She said that the API is down.
Can you say me when it's green? ✗ → Can you tell me when it's green?
They said us to wait until Monday. ✗ → They told us to wait until Monday.
Say me the truth about the estimate. ✗ → Tell me the truth about the estimate.
He told to me yesterday. ✗ → He told me yesterday. / He said to me yesterday.

blocks.body_en: These are the ones you need for reporting a call, passing on an instruction and closing a meeting.
blocks.body_es: Estas son las que necesitás para contar una reunión, pasar una instrucción y cerrar una llamada.
examples: The client told us the deadline can't move.
She said the migration finished around three.
Can you tell Diego to rerun the pipeline when he gets in?
Did anyone tell the client that the export is down?
Could you say that in an email so I can forward it?
I told them we'd need another week.
To tell you the truth, the estimate was optimistic.
I just wanted to say thanks for covering my on-call shift.
He didn't say anything about the budget.
Let me tell you what we found in the logs.

lessons.goal_en: Report what the client said without ever saying "he said me".

Pronouns, articles, prepositions and the words that trip you up.

skills.name_en: Present perfect for results and experience
skills.name_es: Present perfect para resultados y experiencia
